overview: The Wattasids governed from Fez in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, after serving as powerful officials under the Marinids. The map has two spellings for this dynasty. Neither its break at 1530 nor the later label’s continuation to 1650 marks the actual lifetime of Wattasid rule, which ended in 1554.

periods.title: Wattasid rule from Fez
periods.summary: A Wattasid ruler secured Fez in 1472; the dynasty later faced expanding Saadian power.

periods.title: Contested ending
periods.summary: Saadian conquest and a brief Wattasid recovery ended with the dynasty’s final defeat in 1554.

items.text: Portugal captured Asilah in 1471, taking members of the Wattasid leader’s family prisoner. A subsequent agreement helped him turn towards Fez, which he entered in 1472. Coastal warfare and dynastic family fortunes were tightly connected.

In 1515, a Portuguese expedition tried to establish a fortified base at Mamora. Wattasid opposition, including artillery served by Christian gunners, forced its withdrawal. The episode complicates any picture of armies divided into perfectly separate religious teams.

Badis on the Mediterranean coast had a ruler from the Wattasid family who operated with considerable independence. A surviving commercial treaty with Venice, dated 1508, shows how coastal rulers could negotiate their own trading relationships.

A treaty is a different kind of surviving object from a fortress: its clauses preserve negotiated arrangements between people who wanted goods and ships to move. The Badis agreement is evidence for one specific diplomatic connection, not proof that all Moroccan ports followed identical rules.

The later writer Luis del Marmol described Andalusian refugees developing gardens, silkworm cultivation and sugar production at Medgara in the late fifteenth century. García-Arenal discusses this account alongside later wartime destruction. It is an attributed historical account, not an excavated inventory of every farm.

Knowledge of court life could cross a change of dynasty. Dakhlia discusses al-Arifa bint Nedjju, a senior woman of the Wattasid royal household, among people who transmitted court customs to the Saadians. Political history included the expertise of palace women as well as male officeholders.

sections.title: Learning, beautiful pages and small change

items.text: Leo Africanus described students at Fez listening while a teacher explained a text and its difficult passages. Students also debated before the teacher. His account of the early sixteenth century survives through later editions and translations, so it should be read as a situated observer’s description.

The same account says earlier college endowments had supported clothing and food, whereas students in his day were left with lodging and relied on other support. The detail makes education’s everyday cost visible: a classroom alone does not feed its students.

A Quran manuscript in Morocco’s National Library, inventory 1304, is assigned stylistically to the fifteenth or sixteenth century. Its pages are green, with seven lines of silver writing and gold chapter headings. A book could be an extraordinary crafted object as well as a text.

Coloured vowel signs and decorative verse markers helped organise that manuscript’s Arabic text. Only part of its original twelve-volume set survives. The missing volumes remind us that a museum object is often a fragment of a much larger historical possession.

An undated silver quarter dirham attributed to Sultan Ahmad’s reign, 1526 to 1545, carries الحمد لله, “praise be to God,” in Arabic. The short sample follows a photographed specimen’s published transcription. Its exact minting year and excavation provenance are not known.

Later history: a Quran copied at Marrakech in 1599 for Muley Zaydan belongs to the Saadian dynasty, not the Wattasids. It is now in El Escorial. This is why a map label persisting into the 1600s cannot safely identify the ruler who commissioned a particular book.

ending.text: Saadian expansion ended Wattasid rule in 1554 after a contested transition. The replacement of the dynasty did not end Fez, its inhabitants or its scholarly and craft traditions. The imported “Watassid Morocco” label continuing to 1650 includes decades of later history and should not be treated as a reliable dynastic boundary.

sources.title: Mercedes García-Arenal: Sainteté et pouvoir dynastique au Maroc
sources.note: Study of Fez and Saadian power; note 4 on Wattasid chronology, note 15 on Marmol’s account of Medgara agriculture and refugees.

sources.title: Jocelyne Dakhlia: La vie morale des sociétés musulmanes
sources.note: Discussion of Wattasid to Saadian transmission of court knowledge, including al-Arifa bint Nedjju and Qasim al-Zerhuni.

sources.note: Fifteenth- to sixteenth-century Moroccan manuscript, incomplete part of a twelve-volume set; silver writing on green paper and gold headings. Dating is stylistic.

sources.title: Numista: Quarter dirham of Abu al-Abbas Ahmad, N480827
sources.note: Photographed collector specimen, attributed to Ahmad, 1526 to 1545; Arabic legends and reference to Album 550. No excavation provenance or minted year is supplied.

sources.title: A Moroccan Amir’s Commercial Treaty with Venice of the Year 913/1508
sources.note: Study of the treaty with the quasi-independent ruler of Badis, a Wattasid cousin; port politics and diplomatic record.

sources.note: Digitized primary account in John Pory’s English translation, edited by Robert Brown, Hakluyt Society 1896; printed pages 424 to 425, lectures and student support. A later English edition of a sixteenth-century account, not a census.
